analysis.one_liner: Shield companies that supply raw materials for medical implants from most injury lawsuits.
analysis.headline: Despite 31 cosponsors from both parties, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten product liability law for companies that sell raw materials and component parts used in medical implants. It would exempt those suppliers from lawsuits over harm caused by an implant, except in three narrow cases, and would make it much harder to sue them at all by requiring specialist affidavits, restricting evidence-gathering, and making patients pay the supplier's legal fees if a claim was found frivolous. Supporters said this was needed because litigation costs were driving suppliers out of the implant materials market, threatening the supply of lifesaving devices. The bill was sent to two House committees, then to a subcommittee, and never went any further.
analysis.who_benefits: Raw-materials and component suppliers to medical device makers would gain near-total immunity from implant-related lawsuits, keeping them in a market they had been exiting because of litigation costs. Device manufacturers would gain a more secure supply of materials. The bill's findings argue that patients would also benefit from continued availability of implants that depend on these materials, though that benefit depends on suppliers passing the protection along through continued supply.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Implant materials suppliers and device makers

how_it_helps.text: Exempts a biomaterials supplier from liability for harm caused by an implant unless the supplier is a registered implant manufacturer, actually held title to and resold the implant, or delivered materials that violated contractual specifications [S3].
Lets a supplier win dismissal of a lawsuit without any evidence-gathering (discovery) until the court rules on the dismissal motion [S3].

Requires patients suing a supplier to file sworn statements from a qualified specialist before the case can go forward, and to pay the supplier's attorney fees if the court finds the claim frivolous [S3].

The bill's own findings state that suppliers had stopped selling materials for implants because litigation costs exceeded the small revenues from medical sales, and that foreign suppliers were refusing to sell into the US market [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by implants would bear the cost: they could no longer sue most suppliers of the raw materials or components involved, would face upfront affidavits and expert requirements to even proceed against a supplier, would have evidence-gathering curtailed, and could owe the supplier's legal fees. State courts' existing remedies would be preempted by the federal rule.

drawbacks.text: A patient hurt by an implant could generally not hold the supplier of the raw material or component accountable; the only exceptions are if the supplier was a registered manufacturer, held title to and resold the implant, or delivered materials that failed contractual specifications [S3].

A supplier escapes liability unless it registered with HHS and listed the implant; if it failed to register, the patient must petition the Secretary of HHS, who has up to 180 days to decide, during which the lawsuit is stayed [S3].
The bill preempts state product liability law and lets the supplier stop all evidence-gathering until a dismissal motion is decided, which could end many cases before patients learn the facts [S3].

The bill's findings concede that suppliers had 'very rarely' been held liable in these suits; the practical effect was therefore mainly to spare suppliers the cost of defending lawsuits, not to change who actually pays for harm [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The concern behind the bill was real: its own findings document suppliers exiting the implant materials market because defending lawsuits cost more than the sales were worth, which genuinely threatened device availability. But the remedy was one-sided. It removed nearly all legal recourse against suppliers, curtailed the discovery patients need to prove a case, shifted fees onto losing patients, and preempted state law — even though suppliers were rarely held liable anyway. A narrower fix targeting only the cost of defending meritless suits could have addressed the supply problem without closing the courthouse door for patients whose implants contained defective materials.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary and Commerce committees, then a month later to a Commerce subcommittee, and no committee or subcommittee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative George Gekas introduced the bill on January 31, 1995, joined by five original cosponsors from both parties [S1].
It was referred the same day to the Judiciary Committee and the Commerce Committee [S5].
On February 21, 1995, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade, and Hazardous Materials — the last action ever taken on the bill [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients kept their existing right to sue implant materials suppliers under state law, since the liability shield was never enacted. Suppliers and device makers, who had sought the shield, remained exposed to litigation costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients who kept their right to sue

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record; sponsorship leaned Republican (25 of 31 cosponsors) but included 6 Democrats, and one Democrat was among the bill's original six sponsors.

industries.note: The bill would have given these companies near-immunity from lawsuits over harm caused by implants, removing the main financial reason they cited for leaving the implant materials market. The gain comes directly at the cost of injured patients' legal claims against them.

Device makers would gain a more reliable supply of raw materials and components, which the bill's findings say were becoming unavailable due to supplier litigation costs. Their own liability was largely unchanged, and they could even conduct dismissal proceedings on a supplier's behalf.

The bill would restrict evidence-gathering, require specialist affidavits before suing a supplier, and force patients to pay the supplier's attorney fees when claims are found frivolous — all of which reduce implant-injury litigation.
